Pneumonia and tuberculosis cause substantial global mortality, and their overlapping features can lead to misdiagnosis and delayed treatment. Artificial intelligence, particularly convolutional neural networks, has shown strong performance in chest X-ray segmentation and disease classification, but medical datasets often lack sufficient size, diversity, and comprehensive annotation.

Prior studies using CNNs, Vision Transformers, ensembles, knowledge distillation, hybrid features, and quaternion networks reported high accuracy for pneumonia or TB detection. However, identified limitations include dataset imbalance and overlap, limited cross-validation, overfitting, poor generalizability across imaging sources, high computational costs, inadequate reporting of class-specific metrics, and failure to handle anomalous or non-X-ray inputs. Many approaches also focus on binary classification, reducing their applicability in real clinical environments.

The study proposes a pretrained CNN-based framework that classifies images as normal, pneumonia, tuberculosis, or non-X-ray. Adding the non-X-ray category is intended to flag outliers and improve reliability and robustness. The dataset is compiled from multiple publicly available sources. The study also plans model evaluation, Grad-CAM visualization, comparison with existing approaches, and deployment discussion.

All data were anonymized, publicly accessible, and authorized for research, so no additional ethical approval was required. The study followed the Declaration of Helsinki and received no public or private funding.

Nike’s Considered strategy sought to integrate environmental responsibility into product design and core business operations. Prompted by supply-chain risks involving fossil fuels, emissions, waste, toxic materials, and water, Corporate Responsibility VP Hannah Jones adopted an “ROI²” approach combining financial and responsibility returns. Nike focused on design because early product decisions could prevent environmental impacts rather than address them later.

In 2005, Nike created the Considered Group to provide sustainability expertise, tools, and support to product teams while leaving implementation responsibility with designers. Its Considered Index, introduced in 2007, rated footwear based on environmentally preferred materials, solvent use, manufacturing waste, and qualifying innovations. Products received internal Bronze, Silver, Gold, or unrated classifications, with Silver and Gold designated Considered. Nike committed to making all footwear meet at least the Bronze standard by spring 2011.

The Air Jordan XX3 became an early high-profile Considered performance shoe, incorporating recycled sneaker content and reduced solvent use. Core Performance successfully embedded the Index into briefs, reviews, employee evaluations, supplier relationships, and a cross-functional task force. Its entire line achieved Silver by summer 2009, while the Dual D Hoop earned Gold through efficient pattern design, preferred materials, reduced tooling, and a single-mold midsole process that lowered costs and solvent use without compromising performance.

Implementation varied across categories. Challenges included higher material costs, margin pressure, limited staff time, aesthetic and durability concerns, unavailable substitutes for some solvent-based processes, factory capabilities, supplier reluctance, and uncertainty about consumer demand. Some consumers associated greener materials with lower performance, while employees generally believed performance and appearance remained purchasing priorities. Nike also debated whether and how to market Considered.

Although employees largely supported the initiative, the Index had limitations and could potentially reward products despite weaknesses in particular areas. Nike also lacked sufficient data to isolate Considered’s environmental and business effects from earlier sustainability, lean-production, and digital-design initiatives. Going forward, Nike planned an apparel index, broader collaboration with suppliers and innovation units, and continued refinement of its tools and implementation strategy.

Chlorothalonil (CLT) is a persistent, toxic fungicide whose environmental removal and detection are important. This study used density functional theory, semi-empirical calculations, and molecular dynamics simulations to examine CLT adsorption on single-walled carbon nanotubes (CNTs) and boron nitride nanotubes (BNNTs) with (8,0), (10,0), and (12,0) chiralities.

For all systems, the most stable configuration placed the CLT aromatic ring parallel to the nanotube surface. Adsorption was moderate physisorption, with interaction strength increasing as nanotube radius increased because reduced curvature improved π-π orbital overlap. CNTs showed stronger adsorption than BNNTs due to their greater polarizability and more broadly distributed π-electron density. Charge transferred from the nanotubes to CLT.

BNNTs had lower adsorption energies and shorter recovery times, supporting reversible sensing and reuse. CNT recovery times increased substantially with radius; the (12,0) CNT had a particularly long recovery time. CLT adsorption caused only minor changes in CNT band gaps and work functions, indicating limited electronic sensing capability. In contrast, BNNT band gaps decreased substantially because new defect levels appeared, producing large changes in conductivity and electronic sensitivity. Work-function sensitivity in BNNTs declined with increasing radius, requiring diameter control for such applications.

Molecular dynamics simulations confirmed stable CLT adsorption in water, with aromatic rings remaining parallel to both nanotube surfaces and no desorption during the simulations. Both nanotube types could remove CLT, but BNNTs were considered more suitable for combined detection and removal. Even for larger nanotubes, the interaction is expected to remain physical adsorption rather than chemisorption.

The ISM Manufacturing Index, or PMI, is a monthly measure of US manufacturing activity based on surveys of purchasing managers at over 300 firms. Its components include new orders, production, employment, supplier deliveries, and inventories, with seasonal adjustments. Survey responses are scored by the formula: percentage reporting improvement plus half the percentage reporting no change. The index is released on the first business day of each month and reflects the prior month.

A reading above 50 indicates expansion, 50 indicates no change, and below 50 indicates contraction. Investors, businesses, economists, and policymakers use the PMI to assess manufacturing health, economic growth, supply chains, demand, inflation risks, and market conditions. It can be combined with GDP, employment, inflation, consumer confidence, and spending data.

Although widely regarded as reliable, the PMI can be affected by seasonal and global factors and may not accurately predict future conditions. It can offer early economic signals because purchasing managers notice changes quickly, but it also reflects past activity, and markets may have already incorporated its information.

Trading strategies may buy stocks when PMI exceeds 50 and sell when it falls below 50. A cited backtest was invested 72% of the time and returned 7.3% annually, versus 8.5% for the S&P 500, while reducing drawdowns. A 12-month holding period following readings above 50 produced an average 10.99% gain with 86% exposure. Low readings worked better for gold, but overall the index was not a strong contrarian or short-term stock-market indicator.

The paper proposes using semantic embeddings as complements to human ratings in psychometric questionnaire analysis. Existing embedding approaches can reproduce questionnaire structures but often fail to generate important negative correlations. The authors introduce Survey and Questionnaire Item Embeddings Differentials (SQuID), which subtracts the average questionnaire embedding from each item embedding to reduce shared linguistic information and reveal negative relationships without domain-specific fine-tuning.

SQuID is evaluated on the 57-item Revised Portrait Value Questionnaire, which measures 19 value dimensions arranged in a theorized circular structure. Five embedding models are compared with human ratings using internal consistency, dimension correlations, multidimensional scaling, and Procrustes transformation. Linq-Embed-Mistral performs best, attaining average internal consistency above the human benchmark. Embedding-based and human dimension correlations correlate at 0.74, while their multidimensional configurations show congruence coefficients of 0.88 and 0.82. The embeddings recover the questionnaire’s broad circular organization, including proximity among related values and separation of motivationally opposed values.

The authors conclude that SQuID-treated embeddings can recover latent questionnaire dimensions at performance comparable to human-rating methods while remaining flexible, inexpensive, scalable, and reproducible. They present embeddings as complements rather than replacements for human participants and suggest applications including questionnaire development and analysis of cultural biases in language models.

Limitations include uncertainty about whether embeddings and human judgments capture the same phenomena, unresolved methods for reverse-scored items, possible questionnaire exposure during model training, and the context-dependent meaning of similarity. Ethical concerns include displacement of crowdworkers, embedding-derived norms being treated as authoritative standards, and disproportionate economic effects on lower-income workers.

The smash concept is a widely used, teachable football passing scheme that attacks outside the hash marks and offers both deep-play opportunities and quick throws. It generally uses hitch routes by outside receivers, corner routes by slots or tight ends, and a running back checkdown.

Smash works well against man coverage, Cover 2, and Cover 4 by creating space for corner routes or allowing the quarterback to high-low the cornerback. It is riskier against Cover 3, where flat defenders may undercut late hitch throws.

In a base 2x2 formation, the quarterback selects one side before the snap based on defensive leverage and cushion. Post-snap, he reads the cornerback: throw the hitch if the defender gains depth, the corner route if the defender stays low, or check down if the read is unclear. Receivers should sell vertical releases before breaking at specified depths.

Variations include a 3x1 version featuring seam, backside dig, and checkdown options against safety adjustments, and a sprint-out version that moves the pocket, slows the pass rush, adds a backside over route, and gives a mobile quarterback a running option.

The Shayona team participated in SMM4H 2023 Tasks 1 and 4, both binary classification problems. Task 1 identified self-reported COVID-19 diagnoses in tweets, while Task 4 identified positive or probable social anxiety disorder diagnoses in posts from r/socialanxiety. The datasets included 7,600 training, 400 validation, and 10,000 test entries for Task 1, and 6,090 training, 680 validation, and 1,347 test entries for Task 4.

After preprocessing text, the researchers compared RoBERTa, fine-tuned COVID-Twitter BERT, and a hybrid BERT-LightGBM approach. The hybrid model used hidden [CLS] tokens from BERT’s final three layers as LightGBM inputs, with hyperparameters optimized using Optuna. For Task 1, validation F1-scores were 0.83 for RoBERTa, 0.89 for BERT, and 0.93 for BERT-LightGBM. The hybrid achieved test precision of 0.949, recall of 0.938, and F1-score of 0.943. Applied unchanged to Task 4, it achieved precision of 0.756, recall of 0.871, and F1-score of 0.809. The authors suggest that Task 4 performance could improve with domain-specific pretraining and further experimentation with extracted BERT layers and layer dimensions.

The speaker accepts the presidency with personal sorrow, gratitude, and a strong sense of responsibility, pledging faithful service. He praises the Republic’s growth, constitutional system, revolutionary heritage, and example of liberty founded on justice.

His administration will not fear territorial expansion when required for national security and commerce, but acquisitions must respect national faith. Foreign policy will emphasize peace, friendly relations, reciprocal trade, protection of American citizens abroad, and opposition to further foreign colonization in the Americas.

He considers large standing armies dangerous and unnecessary, favors a trained Army as the nucleus of a national militia, and commends the Navy. Domestically, he promises integrity, economy, qualified public servants, and appointments based on effective service rather than personal claims. He stresses constitutional limits on federal power and the proper division of authority between the federal government and the states.

He declares preservation of the Union essential and rejects sectionalism and theories that would weaken national bonds. He states that involuntary servitude is constitutionally recognized where it exists, supports enforcement of the Compromise Measures of 1850, and affirms the constitutional rights of Southern states. He hopes sectional agitation will cease.

Finally, he argues that national security depends on acknowledgment of God and warns against experiments threatening the Union, whose dissolution he believes could not be reversed.

NVIDIA’s A100 GPU introduces 2:4 fine-grained structured sparsity, compressing weights by 2x and doubling Tensor Core throughput while producing virtually no inference accuracy loss after pruning and fine-tuning. Third-generation Tensor Cores, improved data sharing, asynchronous memory copies and barriers, and fewer instructions and register accesses increase deep-learning efficiency.

A100 provides 40 GB of HBM2 memory with 1,555 GB/s bandwidth, a 40 MB L2 cache, and 192 KB of combined L1 cache and shared memory per SM. L2 residency controls and Compute Data Compression improve bandwidth and effective capacity. SECDED ECC protects HBM2, caches, and register files, while separate FP32 and INT32 cores permit simultaneous execution.

Multi-Instance GPU technology partitions one A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances with dedicated compute and memory resources, predictable performance, fault isolation, and quality of service. Instances can be subdivided into Compute Instances, support MPS, VMs, containers, and migration, and improve utilization for multi-user and multi-tenant workloads.

Third-generation NVLink supplies 600 GB/s total A100 bandwidth, while PCIe Gen 4 provides 31.5 GB/s per direction on x16 connections and supports SR-IOV. Additional features include improved error containment, hardware JPEG decoding, optical-flow acceleration, five NVDEC units, and faster atomic operations.

CUDA 11 supports A100 capabilities including sparsity, MIG, Tensor Cores, CUDA Graphs, asynchronous copy, asynchronous barriers, L2 residency controls, and cooperative groups. CUDA Graph optimizations reduce CPU launch overhead and inter-kernel latency.

DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs, six NVSwitches, up to 5 PFLOPS, and 4.8 TB/s bidirectional GPU interconnect bandwidth. It can expose up to 56 isolated GPU Instances and scale to large clusters using InfiniBand, Magnum IO, NGC software, containers, and orchestration tools.

NVIDIA’s Ampere-based A100 GPU improves AI and HPC performance through redesigned third-generation Tensor Cores, expanded numerical-format support, structured sparsity, larger and faster memory systems, enhanced interconnects, and workload partitioning. Its 108 streaming multiprocessors contain 432 Tensor Cores, delivering up to 312 TFLOPS of dense mixed-precision FP16/FP32 performance, 2.5 times V100’s Tensor Core performance. A100 supports FP16, BF16, TF32, FP64, INT8, INT4, and binary operations. TF32 enables Tensor Core acceleration for FP32-based AI training without script changes, while FP16 or BF16 mixed precision provides up to twice TF32 throughput.

For HPC, A100 Tensor Cores accelerate IEEE-compliant FP64 computations to a peak 19.5 TFLOPS, 2.5 times V100. Mixed-precision iterative refinement in cuSOLVER showed TF32 as the fastest and most robust tested Tensor Core mode, with a geometric-mean speedup of 2.0 over the FP64 solver and up to 4 times speedup for some large complex matrices.

A100 introduces 2:4 fine-grained structured sparsity, retaining two nonzero values in each four-entry vector. Sparse matrix instructions skip zero-value computation, doubling Tensor Core throughput while compressed weights halve storage and bandwidth requirements. NVIDIA’s pruning and fine-tuning process produced virtually no inference-accuracy loss across evaluated network types.

Memory improvements include 40 GB of HBM2 delivering 1,555 GB/s, a 40 MB L2 cache, and 192 KB of combined L1 cache and shared memory per SM. Compared with V100, A100 provides over 1.7 times HBM2 bandwidth, 6.7 times the L2 capacity, and 2.3 times L2 read bandwidth. Compute Data Compression can improve DRAM and L2 bandwidth by up to four times and effective L2 capacity by up to two times. SECDED ECC protects HBM2, caches, and register files.

Tensor Core utilization is improved through broader warp-level data sharing, fewer instructions and register accesses, asynchronous global-to-shared-memory copies, asynchronous barriers, larger shared-memory allocation, and programmer-controlled L2 residency. CUDA 11 exposes these capabilities alongside accelerated CUDA Graphs, cooperative groups, sparsity, and Multi-Instance GPU support.

Multi-Instance GPU can divide one A100 into as many as seven isolated GPU Instances, each with dedicated compute, cache, memory-controller, bandwidth, and scheduling resources. Instances provide predictable performance, quality of service, fault isolation, and support for virtual machines, containers, and multiple users. Compute Instances can further subdivide compute resources, and MIG workloads can be migrated between compatible instances or GPUs.

Third-generation NVLink provides twelve links and 600 GB/s aggregate bandwidth per A100, twice V100’s total. PCIe Gen 4 supplies 31.5 GB/s per direction over x16 and supports SR-IOV. A100 also adds hardware JPEG decoding, five NVDEC video decoders, an optical-flow accelerator, and faster FP16 and FP32 atomic operations.

DGX A100 combines eight A100 GPUs through six NVSwitches, providing 4.8 TB/s total bidirectional interconnect bandwidth and up to 5 PFLOPS of AI performance in a 6U system. MIG can create as many as 56 isolated accelerators per DGX A100. The system uses CUDA 11, NVIDIA’s container tooling, NGC software, and optimized frameworks and libraries for deep learning, inference, analytics, and HPC.

The ADS868xW devices are 16-bit SAR ADCs with integrated analog front ends, programmable input ranges, precision reference, alarms, and a multiSPI interface. The nominal 4.096V internal reference is selected by clearing INTREF_DIS and requires at least 4.7µF between REFIO and REFGND. REFIO must not directly drive external loads. Solder reflow can shift reference accuracy; placing the device in the second pass minimizes exposure during multiple reflows. An external 4.096V reference is selected by setting INTREF_DIS, with at least 10µF plus a nearby 1µF capacitor on REFCAP. The reference buffer drift is typically 0.5ppm/°C and specified to a maximum of 2ppm/°C over –40°C to +125°C.

The ADC supports single-ended and differential bipolar or unipolar inputs and produces straight-binary output. LSB size equals the full-scale range divided by 2^16.

Input alarms use programmable high and low thresholds with common hysteresis. AVDD alarms have fixed typical thresholds of 4.7V and 5.3V. Active alarm flags clear after conversion unless the condition persists, while tripped flags clear when ALARM_REG is read. Alarm information can be obtained through the multifunction pin, registers, or appended output flags.

The multiSPI interface supports standard SPI, dual-SDO, source-synchronous operation, and daisy chains. A daisy chain of N devices optimally uses 32 × N clock edges, with throughput decreasing as device count increases. The device operates in RESET, acquisition, and conversion states. Reset can perform either application reset or full power-on reset; conversions begin on a CONVST/CS rising edge and use an internal clock.

Data frames begin when CONVST/CS falls and end when it rises. A 32-clock frame accepts a valid command, fewer than 32 clocks permit partial output reads but invalidate writes, and longer frames use the final 32 input bits as the command. Register commands support byte or half-word reads, writes, bit setting, and bit clearing. Output words contain conversion data, register data, or fixed patterns and may include device address, range, alarm, and parity information.

Nine configuration registers control device identification, reset and power, input and output protocols, output formatting, reference and range selection, and alarm status and thresholds. Four SPI modes are supported; SPI-00-S is the default after power-up or reset. Dual-SDO operation transmits two bits per launch edge, while source-synchronous modes output a clock on RVS.

The application example combines an ADS8681W with an eight-channel differential multiplexer for industrial voltage and current inputs. The device settles to 1% within 5µs and accepts signals up to ±12.288V. Programmable alarm hysteresis can reduce false temperature alarms in thermistor applications.

AVDD and DVDD are separate supplies. AVDD requires at least 10µF and 1µF decoupling, while DVDD requires nearby decoupling. NAP and power-down modes reduce consumption at lower throughput. PCB guidance includes separating analog and digital routing, using short ground paths, placing bypass capacitors close to pins, and directly connecting REFCAP capacitors.

The Rate of Change (ROC/PROC) is a momentum oscillator comparing a security’s current price with its price “n” periods earlier: (Current Price − Earlier Price) / Earlier Price. Positive values indicate upward momentum and negative values indicate downward momentum, while zero-line crossings may signal momentum or trend changes. Short lookback periods generate more sensitive, volatile readings and signals; longer periods generate fewer, later signals.

Traders use ROC to identify overbought or oversold conditions, monitor pullbacks, detect divergences, and seek potential reversals. Extreme thresholds vary by security, and markets can remain overbought or oversold for prolonged periods. Divergences can also persist without producing reversals. ROC is best used with market structure and complementary trend indicators such as moving averages or trendlines.

ROC may support short-term, trend-following, range-trading, breakout, zero-line-crossing, and divergence strategies. It generally works better in orderly trending markets than highly volatile ones, where whipsaws and false signals are common. It can be applied to stocks, futures, forex, bonds, and options-related analysis.

Backtests on the S&P 500 ETF found relatively favorable results for a short-period oversold mean-reversion strategy, particularly with four- and six-day settings, though setbacks occurred. Breakout and zero-line-crossing strategies performed poorly, while divergence strategies were not tested because they were difficult to quantify. Overall, the tested ROC strategies underperformed RSI, stochastic, and Williams %R strategies.

Unlike moving averages, which identify trends, ROC focuses on price momentum and swings. Unlike RSI, ROC measures price change directly, whereas RSI estimates momentum using up and down periods. ROC does not directly determine position size or stop-loss levels, but it can contribute to a backtested trading system and indirectly support risk management. Beginners should learn the indicator, build and backtest a strategy, and use it only if testing shows profitability and robustness.

The AMD Geode CS5535 revision A3 specification update lists hardware errata and workarounds. Illegal LBAR values at or above 10000h have no operational effect but must not be used. Automatic clock gating can cause missed PIC interrupts, lost GLIU statistics ASMIs, UART CEIR failures, and unreliable USB register reads; affected clock domains should remain enabled.

Misaligned or dynamically modified PRD tables may create prefetch hazards, and ATAC PRDs must be DWORD-aligned to prevent hangs. UDMA writes may produce CRC errors after a host-terminated UDMA read; ATAC I/O blocking should prevent host terminations. IDE and ATAPI operations must issue PIO command packets before enabling bus mastering. An ATAC SSMI feature fails to block IDE I/O and should not be used.

Byte accesses to PM1_STS and PM1_EN can hang, while BYTE or WORD writes to PMC registers may corrupt registers; use supported access sizes or SMI trapping. KEL defects affect port identification, Snoop-mode state, and AuxOutputFull handling, requiring trap information, state restoration, or interrupt-driven keyboard and mouse management.

Other issues include unreliable synchronous SSMIs, unsupported PIC polling, limited S3 wake sources, RTC read corruption after specific access sequences, blocked LPC I/O during block or demand DMA, LPC transaction aborts, incorrect SMB NEGACK behavior, shortened SMBus data hold time, premature PCI retry termination, GPIO high-bank corruption after suspend, missing low-battery status, and sleep signals remaining asserted when delay counters exceed PM_SED. Workarounds include processor-based SSMIs, PWRBTN# wake circuitry, single-transfer DMA, repeated SMB status writes, read-modify-write GPIO updates, and adjusted power-management delays.

Some defects have little or no expected real-world impact, including artificial back-to-back PCI read failures, fixed 30 ns UDMA DACK timing, and slightly short PCI tVAL timing. AMD provides no warranties regarding the publication and excludes life-support applications.

The lecture examines running dynamics using the spring-loaded inverted pendulum (SLIP), consisting of a body mass supported by a massless spring leg. Comparative biomechanics shows that animals ranging from cockroaches to horses exhibit similar nondimensional running dynamics and relative leg stiffness despite large differences in size and gait. Tendons and other passive elastic structures store energy, improve efficiency, and can provide rapid stabilization.

The ideal SLIP model assumes a massless leg and toe, a lossless spring, conservative flight and stance phases, and instantaneous placement of the leg at a fixed touchdown angle. Although its flight and stance states are four-dimensional, an apex surface of section reduces the return map to apex height alone: horizontal position does not affect the dynamics, vertical velocity is zero at the apex, and horizontal velocity follows from total energy. The trajectory is mapped from apex through touchdown, stance, takeoff, and the next apex.

Stance dynamics lack a closed-form solution, but small-angle and small-displacement approximations yield an analytical return map with stable and unstable fixed points. Thus, a conservative, piecewise-holonomic system can show passive stability through coordinate switching, although linearization may introduce apparent energy nonconservation. Failure occurs when a low trajectory prevents the leg from being placed before landing.

Models with toe mass lose energy at impact and require energy input, such as varying spring stiffness, but retain similar fixed-point behavior. SLIP-like dynamics also describe lateral cockroach motion. Experiments applying sudden perturbations found recovery faster than neural reflexes, suggesting passive musculoskeletal “preflexes.”

Raibert’s spring-legged robots demonstrated robust running, flips, stair traversal, and quadrupedal motion. Related SLIP walkers can transition between rigid-legged walking and compliant running. Human transitions from walking to running occur where running becomes less energetically costly than walking.

The strategy rotates monthly between the S&P 500 and gold using their price ratio and a 20-month moving average. When the ratio is above the average, it holds the S&P 500 the following month; when below, it holds gold. Backtested from 1985 to July 2020, it produced a 9.9% CAGR and a 22% maximum drawdown, compared with the S&P 500’s 55% maximum drawdown. It lagged the index until the 2008–09 financial crisis, when its lower drawdown enabled stronger subsequent compounding. Gold and the S&P 500 contributed roughly equally to gains, and the strategy reportedly outperformed buy-and-hold in both assets. Repeated cross-sectional surveys measured SARS-CoV-2 antibodies among pregnant women attending first antenatal care visits in four Zambian districts from September 2021 to September 2022. Of 9,221 enrolled women, 8,304 had valid antibody results linked to questionnaires. Overall, 63.8% were seropositive, while reported prior COVID-19 was uncommon.

Adjusted seroprevalence rose to nearly 100% by August 2022 in Lusaka, Chipata, and Chongwe. In rural Chadiza, it peaked at 77.2% in April 2022 before declining to 56.6% in July. The largest increases coincided with or followed Zambia’s Omicron wave. Vaccination coverage increased from 4.4% to 26.6% during the study.

Among participants with anti-RBD antibodies and valid vaccination status, 77.7% had likely infection-induced antibodies, 20.6% had evidence of both vaccination and infection, and 1.6% had vaccination-induced antibodies alone. Combined vaccination and infection produced stronger RBD antibody responses than either alone. Vaccination was associated with higher odds of seropositivity in all districts.

An estimated 2.9 million people in the four districts had evidence of exposure, compared with 90,150 reported cases. Estimated infections exceeded reported cases by ratios ranging from 29:1 in Lusaka to 92:1 in Chongwe.

The study demonstrates substantial geographic variation and the feasibility of integrating serosurveillance into routine antenatal services. Limitations include non-systematic district selection, restriction to pregnant women, antibody waning, possible test misclassification, and the cross-sectional design.

This study assessed circulating tumor cell (CTC) genomic variation as a prognostic marker in 29 metastatic colorectal cancer patients using whole-exome sequencing of CTC pools and matched blood controls. Among 28 microsatellite-stable cases, genomic diversity varied substantially. Multivariate analysis found that high mutant allele tumor heterogeneity (MATH) scores and non-silent BCL9L mutations independently predicted poorer overall survival. Median survival was 18.3 versus 52.9 months for high- versus low-MATH patients and 14.5 versus 34.2 months for patients with versus without BCL9L mutations. A custom 55-gene panel produced MATH estimates correlated with whole-exome results and predicted survival, while two commercial panels did not. The small cohort limits generalizability, requiring validation in larger studies.

BerkeleyGW advances exascale quantum many-body materials simulation through portable, optimized implementations across AMD, Intel, and NVIDIA GPUs. It supports GW calculations of quasiparticle excitations, GW perturbation theory for correlated electron-phonon coupling, accelerated full-frequency GW using static subspace compression, and a mixed stochastic-deterministic pseudobands method that reduces computational scaling.

Directive-based OpenACC and OpenMP provide a unified portable codebase, while HIP, SYCL, and CUDA kernels maximize architecture-specific performance. Optimized diagonal and off-diagonal self-energy kernels demonstrate strong and weak scaling to nearly full Frontier and Aurora systems. The off-diagonal kernel reformulates contractions as dense matrix multiplications, achieving 1.069 ExaFLOP/s on all 9,408 Frontier nodes, or 59.45% of theoretical peak, and 707.52 PetaFLOP/s on 9,600 Aurora nodes, or 48.79% of attainable peak.

Applications include silicon divacancies with up to 2,742 atoms, lithium hydride defects with up to 17,574 atoms, and defective twisted boron nitride bilayers. These developments enable large-scale predictive calculations of excited-state properties and electron-phonon phenomena in heterogeneous materials containing thousands to tens of thousands of atoms.

ABXLAB is an open-source framework for studying how choice architecture affects LLM agents in realistic web environments. It intercepts and modifies web content before agents see it, enabling controlled experiments on ratings, prices, presentation order, and nudges such as authority cues, social proof, scarcity, negative framing, and incentives.

The study evaluated 17 language models in an online shopping environment across more than 80,000 trials. Agents selected between comparable product pairs under original, rating-matched, and rating-and-price-matched conditions. Additional experiments examined explicit user preferences, human baselines, and sensitivity to varying price and rating differences.

Agents displayed substantial and systematic sensitivity to ratings, prices, order, and nudges, often exceeding human responses by three to more than ten times. Higher ratings increased selection probability by 30–80 percentage points across most models. Preferences for cheaper products intensified when ratings were matched, sometimes becoming nearly deterministic. Most models also showed significant order effects in matched conditions, though their direction and magnitude varied. When ratings and prices were matched, nudges shifted choices by roughly 10–60 percentage points across most models. Wirecutter authority cues, “Buy 1 Get 1 Free,” and “best seller” language were especially influential.

Human participants showed comparatively modest effects: 4 percentage points for order, 5 for ratings, 9.4 for price, and 9.9 for nudges. Explicit user profiles strongly reconfigured agent choices, often acting as categorical switches that suppressed competing attributes rather than producing gradual adjustments.

The findings suggest current agents rely on brittle, hierarchical decision rules and can be disproportionately influenced by superficial cues. However, the experiments used binary textual choices in one consumer domain, limiting direct generalization to larger, multimodal, or different decision settings. ABXLAB is intended as a controlled measurement platform rather than a prediction of long-term market or societal outcomes.

First Solar became the largest and lowest-cost photovoltaic manufacturer through proprietary thin-film cadmium telluride technology, achieving manufacturing costs below $1 per watt in 2009. By 2011, however, it reported a $39 million net loss on $2.7 billion in revenue, as growth slowed and its cost advantage weakened.

The solar industry faced declining demand, reduced European subsidies, limited project financing after the global financial crisis, and substantial excess capacity. Meanwhile, falling silicon prices benefited crystalline-silicon competitors but not First Solar. Chinese manufacturers, supported by government programs and lower plant costs, expanded from less than 1% of global production in 2001 to nearly 60% by 2012. Their large-scale output and low prices contributed to falling panel prices and several U.S. solar bankruptcies.

Crystalline silicon accounted for about 85% of solar panels, offering higher conversion efficiency, while thin-film panels used far less semiconductor material and were generally cheaper. First Solar’s manufacturing cost remained lower than major competitors in 2011 at $0.75 per watt, compared with $1.16–$1.48 for Yingli, Suntech, and SunPower. However, First Solar operated below capacity, producing 1.7 gigawatts despite capacity of 2.5 gigawatts.

Solar demand depended heavily on policies such as feed-in tariffs, renewable portfolio standards, tax credits, and net metering. Residential and commercial buyers emphasized lifetime electricity costs, installation costs, efficiency, and reliability. Utilities also valued installation records and, where land was limited, power generated per area. The utility segment was expected to grow from 31% of the market in 2011 to 40% by 2020.

Beginning in 2007, First Solar acquired system integrators and project developers, expanding beyond module production into engineering, construction, operations, maintenance, development, and financing. Systems grew from 5% of sales in 2009 to 25% in 2011. Vertical integration helped overcome customer growth constraints, increase shipments, and improve system performance, but raised selling, general, and administrative expenses. Components historically produced higher profits, while systems offered more stable margins.

First Solar also pursued lower leverage and held more cash than competitors to support customer confidence and project financing. Facing continuing price pressure, falling silicon costs, Chinese competition, and financial losses, management had to determine whether its thin-film cost advantage remained sustainable, whether systems integration was beneficial, and which markets and operations to prioritize.

Alan Oppenheim demonstrates sampling, aliasing, and discrete-time linear systems using a programmable digital filter with adjustable coefficients, word length, and sampling rate. The system samples a continuous-time input, converts it to a sequence, digitally filters it, converts it back, and smooths the result with a low-pass filter.

With the digital filter set to an identity system, sampling creates periodic spectral replications. Exact reconstruction is possible when the input bandwidth is sufficiently small relative to the sampling frequency. Otherwise, spectral overlap causes aliasing. For a sinusoidal input, the reconstructed output frequency initially rises with the input frequency, but after the input exceeds half the sampling frequency, the output frequency decreases according to its alias. Near half the sampling frequency, the nonideal reconstruction filter produces beating.

The demonstration then inserts a symmetric, linear-phase digital low-pass filter with cutoff frequency \(\pi/5\), one tenth of \(2\pi\). The equivalent continuous-time frequency response has the same shape as the digital response, but its frequency axis is scaled by the sampling period. Consequently, the continuous-time cutoff frequency equals one tenth of the sampling frequency.

Measurements show the filter’s symmetric impulse response, the staircase output of the digital-to-analog converter, and smoothing by the reconstruction filter. Frequency sweeps demonstrate passband attenuation, stopband behavior, and the periodicity of the digital frequency response. Changing the sampling rate proportionally changes the effective analog cutoff frequency: doubling the sampling frequency doubles the cutoff, while reducing it narrows the bandwidth. Audio demonstrations at successively lower sampling rates illustrate the resulting loss of high-frequency content before returning to a 40-kilohertz sampling rate.
